It's figuring things out.

I've had plenty of moments where I didn't know how to do something.

A technical problem I couldn't solve.

A design decision I wasn't sure about.

A tool I'd never used before.

Instead of stopping, I learned to break the problem down.

Search.

Experiment.

Ask questions.

Try something.

Break it.

Try again.

That process has become more valuable to me than memorizing another programming concept.

Because technology changes constantly.

The ability to learn doesn't.

A year ago, I wanted to know everything before starting.

Now I just want to know enough to start.

That shift has made a huge difference.

Because there will always be something you don't know.

Another programming language.

Another framework.

Another design principle.

Another business concept.

If you wait until you've learned everything, you'll never actually build anything.

So I've started treating projects differently.

I don't need to know everything before I begin.

I just need to be willing to learn whatever the project demands.

That's probably the most useful mindset I've developed so far.

My obsession with custom loyalty features almost broke our checkout flow.

We were trying to build a unique rewards layer on top of MedusaJS to keep our customers coming back. The logic seemed sound on paper, but integrating it into the core checkout meant overriding default behaviors that were never meant to be touched.

I eventually had to strip back the custom logic and rebuild it as a modular plugin to keep the core codebase stable. Customizing an open-source framework is great until you realize you are fighting against the architecture instead of working with it.

How do you balance adding unique features against maintaining the integrity of your base framework?

Last month, we had a series of payment notifications that simply refused to sync correctly. It turned out that the webhook events were firing in an order I had not anticipated, which left our backend state in total disarray.

I ended up rewriting the entire listener to handle out-of-order events instead of expecting a clean sequence. Learning how to build defensively for third-party API behavior is a skill they do not really teach in tutorials.

Manual data entry for product variants in Odoo is a massive time sink. 

When we were scaling the catalog for Prettiva and Co, I found myself clicking through the interface to create variations for each item. It was repetitive and error-prone, turning what should be a ten-minute task into an hour of administrative frustration. 

I eventually stopped fighting the manual UI and shifted everything to Excel imports. It allowed me to map out all the variants and attributes in a structured grid before pushing them into the system in one go. Sometimes the most advanced software feature you can use is the one that lets you bypass the interface entirely. 

What is the most tedious workflow you have ever automated to save your sanity?
